# RotL 〔BlitzLLVM〕

<div align="center">

[Command Index](Command-Index) · [Language Features](Language-Features) · [Math](Language-Features-Math)

</div>


```blitzbasic
RotL:Int32 value:Int32, count:Int32
```

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | Int32 | required | An integer. |
| `count` | Int32 | required | How many bits to turn by. |

**Returns:** The number with its bits turned.

## Description

**〔BlitzLLVM〕** This command does not exist in the original Blitz products. BlitzLLVM adds it.

<!-- AUTOGENERATED COPYRIGHT HEADER START -->
Turns the bits of a number to the left, and the bits that leave on the left come in on the right. The result has the type of the number, and the count is taken modulo the number of bits, so turning an `Int` by 32 changes nothing and a count of -1 turns it the other way around. This is a BlitzLLVM extension. It looks at the bits of the number the way its type has them, so the same value counts differently as a `Byte`, an `Int` or a `Long`: a number written in the program is an `Int` (32 bits) unless it is larger, and `Byte`, `UByte`, `Short`, `UShort`, `UInt`, `Long` and `ULong` give the other widths. A real or a text is taken as an `Int`, like the bit operators do.

## Differences

* Not in the originals, which have `Shl`, `Shr` and `Sar` only.

## Examples

```blitzbasic
Print RotL(UByte($81), 1)
Print RotL($80000001, 4)
Print RotL(ULong(1) Shl 63, 1)
```

```text
3
24
1
```
